cards.front: Workflow vs agent?
cards.back: A workflow runs LLM calls along code paths you define. An agent lets the model choose its own steps and tools. Use a workflow when the steps are known; use an agent for open-ended problems.

cards.front: Five common workflow patterns?
cards.back: Prompt chaining, routing, parallelization (sectioning or voting), orchestrator-workers, and evaluator-optimizer.

cards.front: What drives the agentic loop?
cards.back: stop_reason: on 'tool_use', run the tools and call again; on 'end_turn', stop and return the answer. Bound the loop with an iteration or budget cap.

cards.front: Why delegate to a subagent?
cards.back: Context isolation: its tool calls and raw results stay in its own context, and only its final message returns. Independent subagents can also run in parallel.

cards.front: Agent SDK in one line?
cards.back: Claude Code's agent loop as a Python/TypeScript library: built-in tools, hooks, subagents, MCP, permissions, and sessions in a process you run.

cards.front: Claude Managed Agents in one line?
cards.back: A hosted agent harness (agent, environment, session, events) in beta. Sessions are stored server-side, so it is not currently ZDR or HIPAA BAA eligible.

cards.front: Memory tool: who stores the files?
cards.back: Your application. The memory tool is client-side: Claude requests file operations and your code runs them under /memories, and it must block path traversal.

cards.front: How do you make a human approval step unskippable?
cards.back: Hold the tool_use in your harness and execute it only after out-of-band approval. The model requests calls; your code decides whether they run.

cards.front: Best reviewer for Claude's own generated work?
cards.back: A second, independent Claude instance without the generator's reasoning. It avoids confirmation bias better than self-review.

cards.front: Where does the system prompt go on the Messages API?
cards.back: In the top-level 'system' parameter, not as a message with role 'system' in the messages array.

cards.front: Is the Messages API stateful across calls?
cards.back: No. It is stateless, so resend the full prior conversation (alternating user and assistant turns) on each request.

cards.front: Headers for a raw HTTP call to the Messages API?
cards.back: x-api-key, anthropic-version (for example 2023-06-01), and content-type: application/json.

cards.front: Why stream long outputs?
cards.back: Streaming avoids idle-connection drops and timeouts on long generations. The SDKs assemble the full message for you (get_final_message() / finalMessage()).

cards.front: How do you return results for parallel tool calls?
cards.back: Put ALL tool_result blocks together in ONE user message. Splitting them across messages discourages parallel calls.

cards.front: Message Batches API: key properties?
cards.back: 50% cheaper and asynchronous. Most batches finish within an hour; a batch expires after 24h and unprocessed requests are not billed. Up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB. Match results by custom_id.

cards.front: Why can't an interactive tool-calling loop run inside a batch?
cards.back: Each batch request is a single call. You can't execute a tool mid-request and feed the result back, so the loop has to run synchronously.

cards.front: Resending the same images every turn?
cards.back: Upload once with the Files API and reference the file_id in image blocks, rather than resending base64 on every request.

cards.front: What changes on Amazon Bedrock?
cards.back: AWS credentials and Bedrock model IDs (for example anthropic.claude-opus-5-5). Some features, such as fast mode, are Claude API only.

cards.front: Project vs personal skill with the same name: which wins?
cards.back: Personal. The precedence is enterprise, then personal, then project. Give a personal variant a different name if you still want the team's version.

cards.front: Personal Claude Code setting in one repo without affecting teammates?
cards.back: .claude/settings.local.json. It overrides the shared .claude/settings.json and stays out of git.

cards.front: How do you share MCP config without committing secrets?
cards.back: Commit .mcp.json with ${VAR} expansion so each developer supplies their own secret. MCP scopes: local (default), project, and user.

cards.front: Why version shared skills and plugins?
cards.back: Consumers can pin a known-good version (plugin dependencies accept semver constraints) and adopt breaking changes deliberately.

cards.front: How should production code name the model?
cards.back: With one exact model ID in versioned config, changed only through an eval-gated review. Every current model ID is a pinned snapshot.

cards.front: How do you prevent drift in a generated content pipeline?
cards.back: Keep one canonical source, generate everything else with a build step, and never hand-edit generated files.

cards.front: What makes a prototype handoff-ready?
cards.back: Evals as gates, docs and runbooks, and shared version-controlled config (CLAUDE.md, .mcp.json, skills) the team can operate.

cards.front: Where does team-wide Claude Code guidance belong?
cards.back: In the committed project CLAUDE.md, which loads for everyone every session. ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is personal, and CLAUDE.md files are combined, not overridden.

cards.front: What scopes a rule to files like tests/**/*.py?
cards.back: A markdown file in .claude/rules/ with a paths: frontmatter glob. It loads only when Claude works with matching files.

cards.front: When does a skill's body load?
cards.back: Only when it's used: when you invoke it with /name, or when Claude decides its description matches the task. Long reference material costs little until then.

cards.front: What does 'context: fork' do in a SKILL.md?
cards.back: It runs the skill in a separate subagent that can't see your conversation history, so verbose work stays isolated and only the result returns.

cards.front: What does disable-model-invocation: true do?
cards.back: Only a user can invoke the skill, and Claude can't trigger it itself. Use it for side-effecting workflows such as deploys.

cards.front: How do you run Claude Code headless in CI?
cards.back: claude -p runs once, prints, and exits. Add --output-format json (or --json-schema for a structured_output field), and --bare for scripts.

cards.front: /clear vs /compact?
cards.back: /clear starts fresh for a new task, while project memory such as CLAUDE.md still loads. /compact summarizes the history so you can continue the same task.

cards.front: Where do shared custom commands live?
cards.back: As files in .claude/commands/ or .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, committed to the repo. Commands have been merged into skills.

cards.front: How should a client handle HTTP 429 and 529?
cards.back: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, honoring retry-after. The SDKs retry twice by default. Don't retry a 400; fix the request.

cards.front: Errors to fix rather than retry?
cards.back: 400 invalid_request_error (for example an unsupported parameter) and 413 request_too_large. They fail the same way on every retry.

cards.front: Empty reply, but the API returned 200?
cards.back: Check whether the code reads content[0].text. Current models can start with a thinking block, so select blocks by type.

cards.front: Role of evals when changing a model or prompt?
cards.back: They are the acceptance gate: run them before any swap and reject changes that regress the eval set.

cards.front: What identifies a request when you contact support?
cards.back: The request-id response header (also exposed by the SDKs). Log it with every error.

cards.front: Default starting model on the Claude API?
cards.back: Claude Opus 5.5 ($4/$20 per MTok, 1M context). Most workloads should start here.

cards.front: Model for the hardest reasoning and long-horizon agentic work?
cards.back: Claude Fable 5.1: the most capable model ($10/$50 per MTok, 1M context, always-on adaptive thinking).

cards.front: Best balance of speed and intelligence?
cards.back: Claude Sonnet 5.5 ($2/$10 per MTok, 1M context).

cards.front: Model for simple, high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks?
cards.back: Claude Haiku 4.5 ($1/$5 per MTok, 200K context, 64K max output). It is the fastest and cheapest.

cards.front: Current context window sizes?
cards.back: 1M tokens on Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, and Sonnet 5.5 by default (no beta header); 200K on Haiku 4.5. Input and output share the window.

cards.front: What does max_tokens limit?
cards.back: The tokens Claude may generate, including thinking. It doesn't cap input or set the context window. Current models allow up to 128K on the synchronous API.

cards.front: What replaced fixed budget_tokens thinking?
cards.back: Adaptive thinking plus effort. Manual budget_tokens is rejected on Opus 4.7 and later; Haiku 4.5 still uses it.

cards.front: How do you adjust reasoning spend without switching models?
cards.back: output_config.effort: low, medium, high, xhigh, max. Opus 5.5 defaults to medium; most other models default to high.

cards.front: Are temperature and top_p available on the newest models?
cards.back: No. Non-default temperature, top_p, or top_k returns a 400 on Opus 4.7 and later. Steer with prompting and effort.

cards.front: How do you count tokens exactly for Claude?
cards.back: POST /v1/messages/count_tokens. The tokenizer introduced with Opus 4.7 counts differently from older models, so rules of thumb drift.

cards.front: stop_reason values?
cards.back: end_turn, tool_use, max_tokens, stop_sequence, pause_turn (a server-tool loop hit its iteration limit), refusal, and model_context_window_exceeded.

cards.front: Prompt caching: match type and ordering rule?
cards.back: Prefix match in the order tools, then system, then messages. Any change invalidates everything after it, so put stable content first.

cards.front: How do you mark cached content, and what does it cost?
cards.back: cache_control {type: 'ephemeral'} on a block (up to 4 breakpoints) or once at the top level. 5-minute TTL by default, 1 hour optional. Writes cost 1.25x (5m) or 2x (1h); reads cost 0.1x base.

cards.front: How do you verify a prompt-cache hit?
cards.back: usage.cache_read_input_tokens. A non-zero value means the cache was read; cache_creation_input_tokens shows writes.

cards.front: Common silent cache invalidators?
cards.back: Timestamps or UUIDs in the prefix, unsorted JSON keys, reordered tools, and changes to tools, tool_choice, thinking, or effort.

cards.front: Fast mode in one line?
cards.back: speed: 'fast' with a beta header, a research preview on Opus 5.5 and select Opus models, on the Claude API only. Higher output speed at a premium price, and not available with batches.

cards.front: Better than more prose for a stubborn output format?
cards.back: Concrete few-shot input-to-output examples: show, don't tell.

cards.front: How do you keep a document from being read as instructions?
cards.back: Wrap it in named XML tags, put long inputs above your instructions, and state that the tagged content is data to analyze.

cards.front: Can you prefill the assistant turn on current models?
cards.back: No. Assistant prefill returns a 400 on the 4.6+ family. Use structured outputs or instructions instead.

cards.front: How do you force a schema-valid JSON response?
cards.back: Structured outputs: output_config.format with type json_schema. Unsupported: min/max, string length limits, pattern, and recursive schemas.

cards.front: What do structured outputs NOT guarantee?
cards.back: Correctness. Validate ranges and cross-field rules in code, and check claims against a trusted source before acting on them.

cards.front: Two server-side context-management tools for long runs?
cards.back: Compaction (older turns replaced by a summary) and context editing (clear_tool_uses removes stale tool results past a trigger).

cards.front: Why not fill the 1M window 'just to be safe'?
cards.back: Context rot: accuracy and recall degrade as token count grows. Retrieve only what each request needs.

cards.front: Core prompt-injection principle for tool and retrieved content?
cards.back: Treat it as untrusted DATA, never as instructions. It must not override the system prompt or authorize actions.

cards.front: Three layers of a defense-in-depth safety stack?
cards.back: Input screening, output screening, and tool-call authorization for high-impact actions, failing closed on uncertainty.

cards.front: What does allowed-tools in a skill actually do?
cards.back: It pre-approves the listed tools for the invoking turn; it does NOT restrict. To block tools, use disallowed-tools or permission deny rules.

cards.front: Which hook blocks a tool call, and how?
cards.back: PreToolUse: return permissionDecision 'deny' or exit with code 2. Permission rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow.

cards.front: Which hook normalizes third-party tool output?
cards.back: PostToolUse. It runs after the tool and can replace what Claude sees with updatedToolOutput.

cards.front: Handling secrets and regulated data (PII/PHI) in prompts?
cards.back: Don't send them without authorization; redact them or use approved compliant channels. Base64 is not protection. Keep API keys in env vars or a secret manager, never in the repo.

cards.front: Primary signal Claude uses to choose a tool?
cards.back: The tool's description. Fix wrong tool selection first by stating what the tool does, when to use it, and how it differs from other tools.

cards.front: Three parts of a tool definition?
cards.back: name, description, and input_schema (a JSON Schema for the arguments). Optional: input_examples and strict.

cards.front: tool_choice on current models?
cards.back: auto (default) and none work. Forced 'any' or 'tool' returns a 400 on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Fable 5.1. Use auto with strict: true, or structured outputs.

cards.front: How do you guarantee valid tool arguments?
cards.back: Set strict: true on the tool so generated inputs always match its input_schema.

cards.front: How do you report a failed tool call?
cards.back: Return a tool_result with is_error: true and a clear message. Never drop it, or the tool_use is left unanswered.

cards.front: What links a tool_result to its tool_use?
cards.back: The tool_result's tool_use_id matches the tool_use block's id. Order is not authoritative.

cards.front: MCP primitives and transports?
cards.back: Primitives: tools, resources, and prompts. Transports: stdio (local) and Streamable HTTP (remote); the older SSE transport is deprecated.

cards.front: Server vs client in MCP?
cards.back: The server exposes capabilities (tools, resources, prompts); the client, such as Claude Code, consumes them.

cards.front: How do you distribute a bundle of skills and commands to teammates?
cards.back: Package them as a plugin and publish it to a marketplace (catalog in marketplace.json). Teammates add the marketplace and install.
